name: Isotretinoin
lead: Isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid), sold as Accutane, Roaccutane, Absorica, Claravis and many other brands, is an oral retinoid related to vitamin A. Its appearance payoff is through the skin: by shrinking sebaceous glands and cutting oil output, it is used to clear severe, cystic, scarring or treatment-resistant acne, which in turn is associated with fewer active lesions, less new scarring and visibly less shine and congestion on the face [1][2][3][4]. Many people in appearance communities describe the end result as a more even, matte complexion, and dermatologists note that most of the visible change comes from clearer acne and lower oil rather than any separate glow effect [37].

It is approved in the United States for severe recalcitrant nodular acne unresponsive to conventional therapy, including oral antibiotics, and dermatologists also use it for moderate acne that scars, resists other treatment or causes psychological distress, and for conditions such as harlequin ichthyosis [1][2][3]. The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology guideline strongly recommends oral isotretinoin for acne that is severe, that carries a psychosocial burden or scarring, or that fails standard oral or topical therapy [4].

The drug was developed at Hoffmann-La Roche, patented in 1969 and approved by the FDA in 1982 [1][7]. It is a potent teratogen carrying a boxed warning, and in the United States it is dispensed through the iPLEDGE risk-management program [1][3][36]. Common effects are dry lips, skin and eyes and sun sensitivity, and the label also carries psychiatric warnings; reviews of prospective studies and meta-analyses describe the depression association as reassuring, while other adverse effects, such as sexual dysfunction reported to the UK regulator, have drawn regulatory notices [1][3][6]. It is available by prescription only.

Isotretinoin has an unusually large public profile for a prescription drug: a long history of litigation and regulation, a distinctive before-and-after genre on TikTok and YouTube, bodybuilding-forum discussion of acne during anabolic steroid use, and online debate over lower-dose courses and claimed secondary effects such as a slimmer-looking nose [1][31][38][39].

paras: The route from drug to appearance is the skin. Isotretinoin is reported to affect all four main processes in acne: sebum production, abnormal follicular keratinization, the skin bacterium Cutibacterium acnes, and inflammation [1][2]. Patients who respond typically see fewer inflamed lesions and less new post-acne scarring, and many describe less facial oiliness and a smoother-looking surface [37].

Dermatologist Rachel Ho writes that the so-called Accutane glow mainly reflects acne clearance and reduced oil rather than a unique glow mechanism, that pores look less noticeable when oil falls but do not disappear, and that the drug does not resurface established acne scars [37]. She also notes that remission can last for years but that acne can relapse and oil may return after treatment ends [37]. Skin on the drug is fragile and heals slowly, and Wikipedia notes that elective skin procedures are discouraged during treatment [1].

Network meta-analyses and reviews place oral isotretinoin relative to topical and other oral treatments, and a network meta-analysis of 221 randomized trials compared the efficacy of pharmacological acne treatments [11][12][13].

The main use is persistent cystic or nodular acne. It is not indicated for prepubertal acne and is not recommended under age 12 [1]. A 2023 review notes that since FDA approval in 1982 for severe recalcitrant acne it has also been used off-label for mild to moderate acne, inflammatory conditions, genodermatoses and skin cancer, with some off-label uses successful and others ineffective [7].

Other uses described by Wikipedia include hidradenitis suppurativa, some severe rosacea, ichthyoses, keratoses in xeroderma pigmentosum, and, in Japan, pediatric neuroblastoma [1]. In oncology, isotretinoin has been part of randomized trials in high-risk neuroblastoma and in medulloblastoma [8][9][10].

Werner Bollag at Roche studied 13-cis-retinoic acid in the 1960s as a possible skin-cancer treatment, and the compound was patented in 1969 [1]. By about 1971 Roche judged it unlikely to work against cancer but potentially useful for acne, and the company set it aside over birth-defect concerns that the thalidomide episode had heightened [1].

In 1975 Gary Peck, a dermatologist at the National Cancer Institute, began collaborating with Roche, and in 1979 Peck and colleagues reported prolonged remissions of severe cystic and conglobate acne in the New England Journal of Medicine; Roche then filed a New Drug Application [1]. The FDA approved the drug in 1982, and Roche had excluded pregnant women from its trials [1].

The FDA warned blood banks against accepting donations from people taking the drug in 1983 and required a boxed warning in 1985 [1]. The NEJM study of 154 exposed pregnancies published in 1985 reported 21 malformed infants among the outcomes [22]. By early 1988 about 1,000 birth defects had been attributed to the drug; an advisory committee urged restrictions, but the FDA expanded warnings and informed-consent requirements instead [1].

In 2000 the CDC reported that Roche's pregnancy-prevention program had not been effective, and congressional hearings followed [1]. The FDA introduced the sticker-based SMART system in 2001-2002, and the iPLEDGE program replaced it on 1 March 2006 [1][36].

subs.h: Litigation and the end of the Accutane brand
paras: Roche's patents expired in February 2002, opening the market to generics [1]. In 2007 Bloomberg reported that Roche had been found liable in the first of about 400 lawsuits, and many suits alleged inadequate warning of inflammatory bowel disease and other harms [1]. In June 2009 Roche announced it would discontinue and delist Accutane in the US, amid falling market share and rising litigation costs, while overseas affiliates continued to sell it as Roaccutane [1]. In 2011 actor James Marshall sued Roche, claiming the drug had led to the removal of his colon; the jury rejected the claim because of his pre-existing bowel disease [1]. The drug remains available under other brand names and generics [1].

The exact mechanism is not established. Isotretinoin is described as shrinking sebaceous glands, reducing sebum output, normalising follicular keratinization and having anti-inflammatory effects, probably partly through sebocyte apoptosis; Wikipedia proposes that induction of apoptosis in other cell types may underlie persistent effects [1][2]. Reviews of its off-label uses cite anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory and antineoplastic properties [7].

It is about 99.9 percent protein-bound, metabolised in the liver and excreted in urine and feces, with a half-life of roughly 21 hours; absorption is better with a high-fat meal [1]. Registered bioavailability and bioequivalence studies of 20 mg and 40 mg capsules in fed and fasting conditions have been run in healthy volunteers [23][24][25][26]. A 1985 controlled letter in the Lancet reported isotretinoin ineffective when applied topically [27].

The AAD guideline's strong recommendation reflects a systematic review with evidence grading [4]. A UK review notes that guidelines generally treat topical therapy as first line and that oral antibiotics are overprescribed, and that regulatory guidance on isotretinoin has implications for specialist prescribing and monitoring [14].

Registered clinical studies include a phase 4 study of two dosages of Roaccutane in cystic acne (91 patients), a phase 4 study of Absorica in severe recalcitrant nodular acne (201 patients), and a planned comparison of low-dose with conventional-dose oral isotretinoin (164 participants) [15][16][17]. Dermatologist commentary on the lower-dose approaches that circulate online notes that they may cause fewer side effects but that pregnancy risk is unchanged and long-term data are limited [37].

The most common effects are dry lips (cheilitis), dry fragile skin, dry eyes and greater susceptibility to sunburn; the label notes that many adverse reactions resemble those seen with very high doses of vitamin A [1][3]. A temporary flare of acne early in a course is also widely described, and 27 of 75 TikTok videos in one analysis mentioned it [39]. A 2022 review describes the dose-dependent mucocutaneous effects as well recognised and easily managed, especially at lower doses, and discusses laboratory monitoring. Liver and lipid monitoring is standard, and liver failure is a reported risk [1][6]. A registered study examined effects on nail plate growth, and another on smell [18][19].

The US label states that isotretinoin may cause depression, psychosis and, rarely, suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, suicide and aggressive behavior, with no established mechanism [3]. Wikipedia reports that proposed mechanisms involve dopamine and serotonin systems and hippocampal neurogenesis, that the UK MHRA received 5,577 reports through March 2017 of which about 22 percent were psychiatric, and that the European Medicines Agency issued a warning in 2018, with causality still debated [1]. In May 2000 Representative Bart Stupak's son died by suicide while taking the drug, prompting congressional hearings [1]. A review of prospective studies and recent meta-analyses describes the data on depression as reassuring [6]. A 2023 JAMA Dermatology meta-analysis examined suicide and psychiatric disorders among users [20].

Wikipedia reports an association with ulcerative colitis but not Crohn disease, and some people develop irritable bowel symptoms [1]. Some effects can persist after stopping, including meibomian gland dysfunction with dry eye, decreased night vision, premature epiphyseal closure in growing people, and hyperostosis [1]. It also notes sexual side effects, erectile dysfunction and reduced libido, an August 2017 EU review and an October 2017 UK MHRA Drug Safety Update, with a possible reduction in plasma testosterone put forward as a plausible explanation [1]. A 2024 systematic review in Cureus catalogues side effects of isotretinoin for acne [21].

The label states there is an extremely high risk of life-threatening birth defects if pregnancy occurs during treatment, even for short periods, and that exposed fetuses cannot be reliably assessed [3]. The 1985 NEJM study of 154 pregnancies with fetal exposure reported 95 elective abortions, 26 infants without major malformations, 12 spontaneous abortions and 21 malformed infants [22]. Wikipedia cites estimates of a 20 to 35 percent risk of congenital defects with exposure [1].

iPLEDGE launched on 1 March 2006 and requires prescribers, pharmacists and patients to register and use its website to prescribe, receive or dispense isotretinoin [36]. Patients who can become pregnant use two forms of contraception (abstinence counts), pass monthly pregnancy tests and a comprehension test, and collect each prescription within a short window; patients who cannot become pregnant attend monthly visits [36].

The program has drawn criticism and study. Wikipedia's iPLEDGE article reports complaints about website glitches and phone waits, privacy concerns about monthly testing, a Children's National Hospital study in which the requirements raised cost and contributed to discontinuation, a 2019 Boston study in which non-white patients had more interruptions and early terminations, and a 2011 study that found no significant reduction in fetal exposure compared with SMART [36]. On 13 December 2021 iPLEDGE moved from sex-based categories to patients who can or cannot become pregnant, a change the AAD had sought, but the AAD said the accompanying system update would slow access to prescriptions [36]. The FDA has also acted against illegal online pharmacies that dispensed isotretinoin outside the program [36].

Acne: the 2024 AAD guideline, the 2021 JAMA review and a 2022 network meta-analysis summarise comparative effectiveness [4][11][12]. Registered dosing studies (91, 201 and a planned 164 patients) are listed above [15][16][17].
Safety: a 2022 review and a 2023 meta-analysis address depression and suicide, and a 2024 review summarises other adverse effects [6][20][21].

Rhinoplasty and nasal appearance: a 2025 PRISMA systematic review in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery found five studies, a median of 24 patients each, with isotretinoin given after surgery in all and before it in two. Two of three prospective studies reported fewer acne lesions, reduced facial skin thickness and higher satisfaction, retrospective studies were mixed, and none reported nasal size reduction; the authors called the evidence limited, with unclear long-term effects [38].

Cancer and other uses: a 2010 New England Journal of Medicine trial in high-risk neuroblastoma tested isotretinoin therapy together with anti-GD2 antibody, GM-CSF and interleukin-2, and a long-term follow-up was published in 2021; a randomized children's oncology trial studied carboplatin and isotretinoin in medulloblastoma; and an oral liquid formulation was tested in a small phase 1/2 neuroblastoma study of 20 patients [8][9][10][28]. A trial in 103 head-and-neck cancer patients and a three-year study in five patients with xeroderma pigmentosum examined retinoid chemoprevention [29][30].

A defining genre is the before-and-after timeline in which creators document months of a course. A Florida State University College of Medicine analysis of 75 TikTok videos found by searching Accutane, presented at the AAD's 2024 meeting, reported that 60 percent mentioned positive effects and 77 percent mentioned negative aspects; side effects featured in 59 percent, led by dry lips (39 percent), dry skin (36 percent) and psychiatric effects (19 percent) [39]. The researchers concluded that positive effects were not the central point in nearly half the videos [39].
Dermatologists following the trend say the visible improvement is real but that it should not be treated as a beauty routine, and that oiliness alone rarely justifies a systemic drug [37].

Posts on TikTok describe a slimmer-looking nose after a course, sometimes called the Accutane nose job. In the 2025 review's analysis of 100 TikTok reels, 90 percent came from patients reporting reduced nasal size and 10 percent from self-identified physicians [38]. Ho writes that research shows some soft-tissue thinning but not changes to cartilage or bone [37].

On T Nation, isotretinoin is discussed by lifters seeking acne control during anabolic steroid use, with accounts of its use as a last resort after antibiotics and topical retinoids failed [31][32][33]. Posts also mention it in long supplement and compound lists and in recovery threads for what some members call post-Accutane syndrome [34][35]. The Wikipedia article reports that some side effects can persist after discontinuation, and describes no defined syndrome by that name [1].

lore.intro: Isotretinoin appears in appearance communities as the drug people reach for when acne has resisted everything else, in transformation videos, and in lifting-forum threads about acne on steroids and perceived lasting effects after a course [31][34][35][39].

claims.claim: Isotretinoin is the last-resort fix for stubborn acne
claims.believers: Members describe trying antibiotics and topical retinoids for years before taking Accutane, which they say cleared their acne [32][33]. Transformation videos present the clearing as dramatic [39].
claims.experts: The AAD guideline strongly recommends it for severe, scarring or treatment-resistant acne [4]. Dermatologists add that relapse can occur and that it does not resurface existing scars [37].

claims.claim: A course gives a lasting 'glow' and permanently smaller pores
claims.believers: Creators attribute a glassy, matte look and smaller pores to the drug.
claims.experts: Dermatologist Rachel Ho says the glow reflects clearer acne and less oil, that pores do not disappear, and that oil and pore size can return after treatment [37].

claims.claim: Isotretinoin slims the nose (the 'Accutane nose job')
claims.believers: TikTok reels, mostly from patients, report a smaller nose after a course [38].
claims.experts: A 2025 systematic review found no included study reporting nasal size reduction, and called the evidence limited; Ho says studies show soft-tissue thinning but not cartilage or bone change [37][38].

claims.claim: Lower-dose or 'microdose' courses give the benefits without the risks
claims.believers: Online posters describe lower-dose courses as gentler.
claims.experts: Ho notes that lower doses may cause fewer side effects but pregnancy risk is unchanged and long-term safety data are limited; a registered trial plans to compare low and conventional dosing [17][37].

claims.claim: Isotretinoin can cause lasting hormonal or libido problems requiring PCT-style recovery
claims.believers: A thread on 'post Accutane syndrome' seeks post-cycle-therapy advice, and another member wonders about hormonal issues after taking it [34][33].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports sexual dysfunction and a 2017 UK regulatory update that cited a possible reduction in plasma testosterone as a plausible explanation; a distinct syndrome is not established in the cited sources [1].

claims.believers: Public concern and TikTok comments cite mood problems; psychiatric effects appeared in 19 percent of videos analysed [39]. The US label lists psychiatric warnings [3].
claims.experts: A 2022 review states that prospective studies and recent meta-analyses have been reassuring, and a 2023 meta-analysis examined the question; regulators including the EMA have issued warnings [1][6][20].

claims.claim: Isotretinoin is safe to combine with anabolic steroids or heavy training
claims.believers: A T Nation thread quotes a member using it while on steroids and drinking [35].
claims.experts: The label directs liver and lipid monitoring and notes liver failure as a reported risk [1][3]. No trial in the cited sources tests combination with anabolic steroids.

claims.claim: The drug caused inflammatory bowel disease
claims.believers: Plaintiffs in lawsuits against Roche alleged inadequate warnings of bowel disease [1].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports an association with ulcerative colitis but not Crohn disease; in the 2011 Marshall case the jury rejected the claim because of pre-existing bowel disease [1].

chain: Shrinks sebaceous glands and reduces sebum output
Fewer inflammatory lesions and less new scarring
angle.text: Isotretinoin is used to clear severe or scarring acne, which changes how the skin looks and limits new scars. Dermatologists describe the lasting change as coming from reduced oil and lesion count, and note that it does not resurface existing acne scars [1][37].
